Try holding the striker lightly with your thumb and one finger and flick with a steady, short motion. A hard swing makes it wobble. Practise by pocketing one coin from the same spot again and again.
I'll try. Do I need talcum powder on the board?
A thin, even dusting of fine powder is how many people prepare a board, because it lets the pieces slide smoothly. Ask your cousins how they do it at home, as they may have a favourite way.
It rained and now there are little paper boats floating in the lane. The kids made them. I'd like to make one too.
That sounds like a perfect rainy-day activity. A folded paper boat is simple to make, and it floats well on a puddle for a few minutes.
Mine always sinks quickly. Why?
Paper soaks up water, so it becomes heavy and slowly sinks. Folding the paper tightly and sealing the bottom edge with a bit of clear tape slows that down.
Does thicker paper work better?
Often, yes. Thicker paper takes longer to soak, so the boat floats for longer. Just make sure it is still easy to fold, or the shape will be uneven.
We have a six-hour bus ride tomorrow, and my little sister gets restless after an hour.
Plan a few small surprises. Pack a snack, a short story to read aloud, and some paper for drawing or word games.
She likes guessing games.
Then you're in luck. You can play 'I spy' out of the window, or twenty questions, where she thinks of an animal and you guess it. These need no equipment at all.
What if she gets bored of those too?

Take turns picking a song to hum, and the other person guesses it. Short breaks to stretch at a rest stop help too. Between games, let her look outside quietly, since travelling can tire a person out.
We'll try them all. Thank you!
You're welcome. I hope the bus ride goes smoothly, and maybe she'll even doze off.
I'm picking a topic for a project and I like rivers, but I don't know what part to choose.
Rivers give plenty of choice. You could focus on how a river is formed, on a river near your town, or on how people have used rivers over time.
I like the idea of a river near my town.
Then you could cover where it starts, where it ends, which places it passes, and how people use its water. A local project is also easy to illustrate with your own photos or sketches.
The problem is I don't know where it starts.

A good place to look is your school library or an atlas, and your geography teacher may know too. Local newspapers and the town library sometimes have old maps, which would also make your project more interesting.
We're running a small lemonade stall for our street fair. Should we sell it plain or add something?
A classic lemonade is easy and popular, but one extra option can make you stand out. Mint is simple and refreshing.
We can do plain and mint. How many lemons should we squeeze?
A rough guide is one lemon per glass, but it depends on how sour people like it. Do a taste test in a small jug first and adjust, then scale up.
Good idea. What should we do about the ice?
Keep it in a covered container so it melts slowly, and use a clean scoop or tongs rather than hands. That keeps everything tidy, and customers will notice the care you take.
I got to school today and realised I'd worn my shirt inside out all morning. Nobody told me.
That's an easy mistake to make, especially on a rushed morning. Chances are most people didn't notice, and anyone who did probably forgot by now.
My friend finally told me at lunch. I felt silly.
It is a small, funny moment, and your friend was kind to tell you. Everyone has a story like this, and some people even laugh about it years later.
Reading in English is my new goal, but difficult words keep stopping me.
Don't stop at every word. Try to follow the story, and underline only the words that come up more than once. Those are the ones worth learning.
What kind of book should I start with?
A short story collection or a book for younger readers can be a good start. Pick something about a topic you already enjoy, so you can guess the missing words from the story.
I like animal stories.
Then you have a clear direction. Animal stories use plain language and lots of repeated words, so reading one will feel easier than you expect.
I'll ask my school librarian. Is it okay to read the same book twice?
Yes. A second reading helps you notice words you missed and lets you enjoy the story at a relaxed pace. Many readers do it on purpose.
Our puppy has chewed my slipper again.
Puppies chew to explore and to ease their teething. It's frustrating, but it is normal behaviour at this age.
How do I stop it?
Keep your things out of reach and give him chew toys that are made for dogs. When he picks up the slipper, calmly swap it for a toy, and praise him when he takes the toy.
Does scolding him help?
Not usually. He may not connect the scolding with the slipper, and it can confuse him. Calm redirection works better, along with plenty of walks and play so he has less energy to spare.
Thanks. He looks so guilty after, though.
Dogs do have expressive faces, don't they? The look is often a reaction to your tone rather than a sign that he understands what happened. Be patient and he will learn.
I made a typo in the title of a presentation and only noticed after sending it to the team.
That's an annoying moment, but a typo in a title is a small problem. It happens to nearly everyone.
Should I send a corrected version?
A short, friendly note with the corrected file is fine. Something like, 'Please use the attached version, I fixed a typo in the title.' That is clear and quick, and no long apology is needed.
Okay. How do I avoid this next time?
Read titles and headings last, after the content is finished, and read them aloud. Your eyes tend to skip over big text, but your ears catch mistakes.
We've got a new balcony and I want to make it a little reading nook.
What a lovely idea. Start with a comfortable seat and a small side table or crate for your tea or book.
The balcony gets hot in the afternoon.
Then use it in the early morning or evening, and think about a light curtain or a plant to soften the sun. Simple cotton cloth works well for shade.
And what about rain? It gets wet in the monsoon.
Keep the cushions in a covered bag or indoors during the rains, and carry them out when you want to sit. A plastic stool or a basket is easy to wipe dry.
That makes sense. What should I read first?
Pick something you've been meaning to read, or an old favourite. A reading nook feels best when the first book in it is a book you really want to open.
My friend wants to share a secret with me, but she says I can't tell anyone. I'm worried it will be something I can't keep.
That's a thoughtful worry. It is fair to listen first and say honestly that you care about her and will try to be a good friend.
What if it's about someone getting hurt?
If someone's safety is at risk, it is right to tell a trusted adult, even if you promised. You can say that kindly to your friend, such as, 'I'll keep it private unless somebody could get hurt.'
That helps. I'd rather say it first than regret it later.
Setting that expectation early is fair to both of you, and it shows you take her seriously.
Whistling is harder than it looks. Nothing comes out of mine except air.
Many people start there. Wet your lips, shape them into a small circle and blow gently. Keep your tongue relaxed behind your lower teeth.
I got a tiny squeak, but it disappeared.
A squeak is progress. Adjust the shape of your lips a tiny bit each time until you find the spot where it rings. It may take a few days of short practice.
Can I learn to whistle a tune after that?
Yes. Once you can hold one steady note, try changing it by moving your tongue slightly. Start with a simple tune you know well, and go slowly.
We're planning a treasure hunt for my little cousins at the Diwali family gathering.
A treasure hunt is a fun idea, and festival lights make it feel special. How old are the children?
Between six and nine.
Then keep clues short and picture-based for the younger ones, and word riddles for the older ones. Pair them up so that nobody feels left behind.
Where should the treasure be hidden?
Somewhere safe and easy to reach, like a basket under a table in the living room. Keep the hunt away from lit lamps and fireworks, so the children can run around without worry.
Good point. What should the prize be?
Sweets to share, small notebooks or a mix of both. A prize that everyone can enjoy together works better than one for the winner alone.
I haven't heard from my old school friend in a year and I want to message her, but it feels awkward.
It's common to feel that way after a long gap, but most people are happy to hear from an old friend.
What should I write?
Keep it light and warm, like, 'Hi Sana, I was thinking of you today and wondered how you are. It would be lovely to catch up.' No need to explain the silence at length.
That's nice. What if she doesn't reply?
People get busy, so give it a week or two without worrying. A reply may come later, and either way you did something kind.
I'm visiting my grandparents in a village for the first time. I'm used to the city and worried I'll be bored.
Villages have their own pace, and many people end up loving it. You could think of it as a calm break from the usual rush.
What can I do there?
Walk around with your grandparents, help with simple chores, watch the evening sky, and ask them for stories. If you carry a book or a sketchbook, quiet afternoons will feel pleasant.
I'd like to hear about my grandfather's childhood.
He will probably love that. Ask small, specific questions, like what games he played or what school was like. Specific questions bring out the best stories.
My room has become a dumping ground for school stuff and I can't focus.
A cluttered desk makes it hard to start. Begin with just the desk and clear everything off. Put back only what you need daily.
Where do I put the rest?
Sort the rest into three piles: keep, store and throw away. Old worksheets can go in a folder, and extra pens in a pencil box. Anything you no longer use can be recycled or passed on.
That seems doable.
Set a timer for twenty minutes, so it doesn't turn into a whole-day job. Then enjoy the clear desk.
My brother keeps humming the same song all day and it's stuck in my head too.
That's the famous earworm. A tune can get stuck simply because you heard it a lot.
How do I get rid of it?
Try listening to a different song all the way through, or chewing gum, or doing something that needs your full attention like a puzzle. Often it fades by itself in a few hours.
Maybe I'll just hum it back at him.
That would certainly share the joy. Just be kind, since he may be enjoying it.
A notice at school had a spelling mistake and my friends laughed. I feel bad for whoever wrote it.
That's thoughtful. People often write quickly, and a small slip is easy to miss.
Should I tell the teacher?
If it bothers you, you could mention it quietly to the teacher, without making anyone feel embarrassed. Say it simply, like, 'I think one word in the notice may need a second look.'
I'll do that tomorrow.
Good plan. A quiet word means it gets fixed without any fuss.
I found a feather on my morning walk and I don't know which bird it came from.
A nice find. Feathers can tell you a lot. Look at its size, colour and shape.
It's long, black and shiny with a slight blue tint.
That sounds like it could be from a crow or a similar black bird, though I can't say for sure from a description. A local bird guide or a nature club can help you check.
I'll look in the library. Is it okay to keep it?
For one feather, it's usually fine, but wash your hands afterwards, since feathers can carry dust and germs. Local rules may differ, so ask at the library or the nature centre if you are unsure.
I got a small cut while peeling vegetables with my mother, and I'm scared of the knife now.
That sounds scary, and it makes sense to feel cautious. Is the cut being looked after by an adult?
Yes, Mom cleaned it and put a plaster on it.
Good. A bit of caution is healthy around knives. When you're ready, you could start again with a peeler and a firm board, with Mom beside you.
Okay. I'll try tomorrow with a peeler.
That's a smart step. Let her show you how to hold the vegetable steady, and go slowly. Your confidence will come back.
I'm halfway through a thick book and want to give up. It's slow.
Slow stretches are common in long books. Ask yourself whether you enjoy the characters or not. That tells you whether to stay.
I like the main character, but the plot isn't moving.
Then maybe give it another thirty pages. Many stories pick up after a slow middle. If it still drags, there is no shame in putting it down.
What if I want to come back to it later?
Keep a bookmark in it and leave it somewhere you'll see it. You may feel differently in a few months.
I'll try thirty more pages. Is it okay to skim?
Skimming a slow chapter is fine, as long as you read the important moments closely. Then you can enjoy the rest at normal speed.
Our rice cooker finishes cooking, but the rice at the bottom always sticks.
Sticking is common. Are you washing the rice before cooking?
Not usually.
Washing removes extra starch, which causes a lot of sticking. Rinse it two or three times, until the water looks less cloudy.
And after cooking?
Let it sit with the lid on for a few minutes, then fluff it gently with a spoon. This helps the steam settle and the grains separate.
I'll try both. Does the amount of water matter?
Yes, it does. Follow the water line in your cooker, or the ratio on the rice packet, because too much water makes rice soft and sticky.
My neighbour's cat sits on our wall every evening and watches us eat dinner.
Cats are good at looking dignified while hoping for a snack. Does she come inside, or only watch?
Only watches. I've never fed her.
That is the safe choice. If you want to be friendly, you could say hello without offering food, and let her come to you. Her family would also like to be asked first.
Right. I'll just wave.
A wave is a polite and safe choice. She may decide you are a friend and settle on the wall a bit closer, with no food needed.
My friend and I both like the same person's band and we argue about which album is best.
A friendly debate is a good thing. What does each of you like about your pick?
I like the lyrics, she likes the beat.
Then you may both be right in different ways. You could each make a list of three songs from your favourite album and swap, listening with open minds.
That's a nice idea. Maybe I'll like hers more than I expect.
It could happen. And if not, you've still shared something, which is half the fun of liking music with a friend.
I'm teaching my little brother to ride his first bike with training wheels. He wants them off already.
Enthusiasm is great. How is his balance when he rides?
Decent, but he still wobbles in turns.
Then you could raise the training wheels a little so he practises balancing, while they catch him if he tips. Do this before taking them off completely.
Where should he practise?
A flat, quiet, open area, like a car-free playground, is best. Have him wear a helmet, and stay close to him.
Great, I'll get a helmet for him first.
Good thinking. Fit matters, so it should sit level on his head with the strap snug but comfortable.
I got a message from a coworker at night asking for a favour. I feel pressure to reply.
It's fine to wait until the morning for something that isn't urgent. Rest is part of doing good work.
What do I say when I reply?
You could say, 'Good morning! I saw your message last night. I can help with that by noon.' It's friendly and clear, and sets your own timing.
That sounds polite without sounding stiff.
Exactly. Short, warm and specific is the easiest tone to keep up.
We're doing a Christmas play at school and I got the part of a shepherd. I don't have much to say.
A shepherd is a lovely part, and small roles often steal the scene with good expressions. What are your lines?
Just two sentences, but I get nervous speaking.
Practise them in the mirror and then to a family member, speaking slowly. Two lines said clearly are better than ten said fast.
What should I do when I'm not talking?
Stay in character. Look at what the others are doing, react to the story and keep your body still when others speak. That makes the whole scene feel real.
I like that. Maybe I can practise looking amazed at the star.
A look of wonder is perfect for a shepherd. You may get the biggest smile from the audience.
I always feel sleepy after lunch at school. Is it normal?
A lot of people feel a dip in energy after lunch. It isn't unusual, though I'm not a doctor. If it bothers you a lot, a school nurse or your family doctor can advise.
What can I do to stay alert?
A short walk, a few sips of water and sitting near a window with fresh air can help. Plan harder subjects for earlier in the day if you can.
I'll try drinking water and stretching in the break.
Good plan. Both are easy to do between classes, and they cost nothing. Notice over a week whether it makes a difference.
My mother says I should help in the kitchen more. I don't know how to start.
That's a nice step. Start with simple jobs, like washing vegetables, laying the plates and stirring.
I'm afraid of making a mess.
A bit of mess is part of learning, and cleaning up is part of the job. Wipe as you go and the kitchen stays calm.
What should I try cooking first?
Pick something with few steps, like scrambled eggs, a simple dal or a sandwich. Ask your mother to guide you the first time, and you will learn the order of things.
Okay, maybe I'll start with a sandwich.
A fine choice. Aim for one tidy sandwich and a clean counter, and call it a success.
Our class is picking a mascot for the sports house. People keep arguing.
Arguments about mascots are very common. What are the main ideas?
A tiger, an eagle and a dolphin.
A quick vote can settle it. Each person gets one vote, and you count together. Before voting, let each supporter speak for one minute.
What if it's a tie?
Hold a second vote between just the tied choices, or let the class teacher pick one. A rule agreed before voting stops the arguing afterwards.
Okay, we'll try a vote. Thanks.
Good luck with the vote. Whatever wins, the mascot will be yours, so enjoy choosing together.
Today I felt proud of myself because I finally finished a hard puzzle.
Well done. A hard puzzle takes patience, and finishing it is a real achievement. How long did it take?
Three days, on and off.
That is solid persistence. Three days of small bits adds up to a finished picture, and you should enjoy that feeling.
I want to do a harder one next.
Go for it, but maybe pick one just slightly harder, so it stays fun. A bigger puzzle can be a good next challenge after a short rest.
We've planted a mango sapling in our yard. How long until it gives mangoes?
Mango trees take their time. A tree grown from a seed may need many years, while some grafted saplings can fruit sooner. The nursery that sold the sapling can tell you more.
Ours is a small grafted one.
Then a few years is a reasonable guess, but it depends on the variety and care. Water it regularly while it is young and protect it from strong winds.
Is there anything I should avoid?
Don't let water collect around the base, and avoid damaging the trunk when you clean around it. Your local nursery can give advice for your area.
Thanks, I'll ask them. I'll make a growth chart too.
Lovely idea. A photo every few months will show how much it grows.
Our flight is at six in the morning, so we have to leave home at three. I'm dreading it.
An early start is hard, but you can prepare. Pack the night before and keep tickets, IDs and chargers in one place by the door.
Should I sleep at all?
Try to go to bed early so you get some rest, even if you only manage a few hours. You can doze on the flight if you feel sleepy.
What about breakfast?
Eat something light before leaving, and carry a snack and a water bottle. Airport food is usually expensive and limited at that time.
I'll pack some fruit. Thanks for the checklist!
Welcome. Fruit and a bottle of water are a smart pair. Have a smooth journey.
My friend moved into my building, and now he comes over every day. I like him but I need space.
It's great to have a friend close by, and it's also fine to want time alone. How often is he visiting?
Almost every evening.
You could tell him honestly, 'I love hanging out, but I need some quiet evenings for homework and rest. Can we pick two or three days?' That keeps things kind and clear.
Do you think he'll be upset?
He may feel a little disappointed at first, but a clear plan usually helps a friendship. When he sees you still want to spend time together, he'll understand.
I joined a football club, but I'm the youngest player. The others are quicker.
Being the youngest means you're learning from people who know more. What part of the game do you like best?
I like defending.
Then focus on positioning and reading the play, because defenders use brains as much as speed. Watch where the older players stand and why.
How can I improve my speed, though?
Short sprints and quick-step drills help over time, and your coach can suggest exercises that suit your age. Gradual progress is better than pushing too hard.
Thanks. I'll ask my coach tomorrow.
Good. Coaches usually enjoy questions from players who want to learn.
A fruit salad for the family lunch is my job this Sunday. Any tips?
Choose fruits that taste good together and cut them into similar sizes. Mixing sweet, juicy and crunchy fruits keeps it interesting.
I have banana, apple and grapes.
Those three work well. Cut the banana last, and squeeze a little lemon over the apple so it doesn't turn brown quickly. Keep the grapes whole or halve them.
Should I add sugar?
Taste it first. Ripe fruit is often sweet enough already. A drizzle of honey or a little chaat masala is a tasty option if you want more flavour, but only if the family likes it.
They'll love chaat masala. Thank you!
Then they're in for a treat. Add it just before serving so the fruit stays fresh and crisp.
I'm starting a reading corner for my class. What should I put in it?
A mix of books keeps everyone interested. Include picture books, short stories, a few facts-and-pictures books and a comic or two.
Where do I get so many books?
Ask classmates to donate a book each, and check with your teacher about borrowing from the school library. A swap shelf also works well.
How do I stop people from losing books?
Make a simple sign-out list on a sheet of paper: name, book, date. Appoint a different student each week to check it.
Smart. Should the books go on a shelf or in a box?
A shelf with covers facing out looks more inviting. If there is no shelf, a low box that children can reach easily is fine.
My teacher wants me to practise scales every day, but they're boring.
Scales are the foundation for everything else, but you can make them more fun. What instrument do you play?
Keyboard.
Try playing scales with different rhythms or speeds, or play them with your eyes closed once you know them well. You can also make a game of beating your own tempo.
Does it really help?
Yes, it builds finger control and helps you recognise patterns in songs. Just ten minutes a day is enough.
Alright, I'll try the rhythm game today.
Have fun with it. Start slowly with a rhythm you can tap easily, then speed up as you get comfortable.
The wall behind my bed has a patch of peeling paint and it bothers me.
That's annoying to look at. Is it dry, or is the wall damp?
It's dry, just old.
Then it's probably just old paint. A grown-up can scrape off the loose bits and paint over them. Ask your parents before starting, since there may be dust.
Could I hang a poster over it instead?
For now, yes. A poster or a cloth hanging can cover it nicely. Use tape or hooks that won't damage the wall, and ask your parents first.
Good idea. I have a nice map poster.
Then it could look great, especially if it is a bright one. Hang it a bit above the bed so the spot is covered and it still looks tidy.
My teacher gave us a worksheet with twenty questions and I got stuck on number five.
Getting stuck is a normal part of studying. What kind of question is it?
A word problem on distance and speed.
Try reading it slowly twice and writing down what is given and what is asked. Sometimes a simple diagram shows the answer.
I wrote down the facts but I don't know what to do next.
Think about which formula links the facts you have. If you aren't sure, check your notebook for a similar solved example. If you still can't see it, mark it and ask your teacher tomorrow.
Good, I'll mark it and move on to number six.
That is a smart move. Leaving a hard one for later often lets your brain work on it in the background.
I found my dad's old stamp album in the cupboard. It's full of stamps from many countries.
What a treasure. Old albums often hold small stories. Before you touch anything, wash and dry your hands, since fingers can leave marks on paper.
Done. Some stamps are stuck to the pages. Should I peel them off?
No, please leave them stuck. Pulling can tear them, and the album itself is part of the collection. If you are unsure, ask your dad how he arranged them.
He says he started it when he was twelve. I never knew.
That is a lovely thing to discover about him. You could ask which stamp was his first or his favourite. Collectors usually enjoy telling those stories.
He pointed to a blue one from a country far away. He said it came in a letter from a pen friend.
Then that stamp has a story behind it. You could write a small label next to it with the year and the name of the pen friend, so the story stays with the stamp.
I'll write the label in pencil, so it can be changed. Thanks for the idea.
Pencil is a gentle choice because it can be erased. Keep the album somewhere dry and flat, and it will stay in good shape for years.
I'm organising a farewell lunch for a colleague who is retiring, and nobody has volunteered to help.
That's kind of you to take it on. Even a small team of two or three makes it easier. You could send a short note asking who can help with one task each.
What tasks should I list?
Choose a venue or a spot in the office, collect small contributions, order or bring food, and arrange a card for everyone to sign. Four simple jobs are easy to share.
People keep forgetting to sign cards. Any ideas?
Leave the card on a desk where people pass often and tell the team on which day it will go to the retiree. A friendly reminder the day before helps too.
The lunch is on Friday. Should I keep it a surprise?
If your colleague likes surprises and you know someone close who can bring them to the room, it can be lovely. If you aren't sure, ask her manager or a close friend what she would prefer.
Her manager says she'll be thrilled. I'll plan a small speech too.
Keep it short and personal. Two or three warm memories, a thank you and a good wish for her next chapter are enough.
Why does the sky turn orange at sunset? My little brother asked and I couldn't explain.
Here is the short version. Sunlight looks white but contains many colours. In the evening, the sun is low, so its light travels through more air before reaching you.
And what does the air do to it?
The air scatters the blue light away, so mostly the reds and oranges remain. That is why the sun and nearby clouds look warm in colour.
How do I say it to a seven-year-old?
You could say, 'Sunlight has lots of colours hidden inside. At sunset the blue ones get lost on the long way, and the orange ones reach us.' Short and simple works best.
He asked why the sky is blue in the daytime then.
In the daytime the light has a shorter path, and the air scatters blue light across the sky in all directions. So blue comes to your eyes from everywhere you look.
That actually makes sense now. Thanks for the clear explanation.
Glad it helped. Next time you see an orange sky, you can both look for how the colours change from the sun outwards.
My deskmate spreads her things all over our shared desk, and I end up with no space.
That's annoying when you need room to write. A friendly word at the start usually works best. You could say, 'Can we each keep to our own half of the desk?'
What if she forgets after a day?
Then a small marker helps. Place a ruler or pencil box along the middle as a gentle line, and point to it with a smile when things drift across.
I forgot my new classmate's name twice already, and it's too late to ask again.
It happens often with new names. Most people would rather be asked than be called by the wrong name, so a quick 'Remind me of your name once more?' is fine.
Won't she be offended?
Usually not. It shows you want to get it right. You can add a small trick, like repeating her name once in your reply, so it sticks.
Our class is starting a wall magazine and we need a name for it.
A fun project. Think about what your class is like. Are you mostly jokers, artists, readers or sports fans?
A bit of everything, honestly.
Then a name that suits many things could work, such as 'The Mixed Bag' or 'Class Corner Chronicle'. Collect ideas in a box and let everybody vote.
I'm getting a haircut tomorrow, a short one, and I'm a little nervous.
A new haircut is a small adventure. Do you have a picture of the style you want?
I do, but my hair is thicker than the model's.
Then show the picture to the hairdresser and mention your hair type. A good hairdresser will tell you how close it can look. Hair also grows back, so there's no need to worry too much.
I'm trying to read sheet music for the first time and the notes all look the same.
They start to look different with a little practice. Begin with just the notes in one clef and learn their names, one or two at a time.
Is there an easy way to remember them?
A rhyme can help. Many learners use a short sentence where each word's first letter is a note name. Make up your own, and it will be easier to remember.
I walk with my grandfather in the evenings, but he walks slowly and I get impatient.
It's honest of you to notice that. Slow walks have their own gifts, because you can talk without hurrying.
What should we talk about?
Ask him about the lanes he walked as a boy, what changed in the neighbourhood, or what he loves most about evenings. He may enjoy being asked.
Teachers' Day is on Friday, and our class wants to do something nice for our class teacher.
What a thoughtful plan. A handmade card with a message from every student is simple and personal.
We also thought of singing something. Is that too much?
Not at all, as long as it is short and warm. One song and a card are plenty, and she will remember it for a long time.
Weeds are taking over our vegetable patch. I pull them out and they come back in days.
Weeds are persistent. Pulling them with the roots after rain, when the soil is soft, helps them stay away for longer.
Should I put something on the soil?
A layer of dry leaves or straw on the soil, called mulch, blocks sunlight, so fewer weeds grow. It also keeps the soil moist.
The cookies I baked came out dark on the bottom and soft on top. I followed the recipe!
That's disappointing after the effort. A common cause is that the tray was too close to the heat at the bottom, or the oven was hotter than the dial says.
Should I move the tray higher?
Try the middle level next time, and check them a few minutes before the recipe's time. Every oven behaves a bit differently, so you'll learn yours.
The lift in our building is out of order again, and I live on the fifth floor.
That's a long climb with bags. Is there a way to carry things in smaller loads?
I can split the shopping, but it takes many trips.
Then make a game of it. Take the heaviest bag first, rest on landings, and bring the lighter ones afterwards. Stretching your legs a bit afterwards helps too.
We're going to a restaurant that serves food with chopsticks and I've never used them.
A fun experience. Hold the upper stick like a pencil, and keep the lower one steady between your thumb base and ring finger.
I'll probably drop everything.
Most beginners do. Practise at home with something easy, like a few peanuts, before you go. And restaurants usually have forks if you need them, so there's no pressure.
My jacket zipper is stuck, and I'm already late for school.
Don't force it, or it may tear the cloth. Look to see whether some fabric is caught in the teeth.
There's a bit of cloth caught.
Hold the cloth gently away from the zip while moving the slider back a little. If it still won't move, rub a pencil tip along the teeth and try again.
We're attending a cousin's wedding where I'll meet lots of relatives. I always get confused about manners.
Relatives are usually happy if you are polite and warm. Greet elders with a hello or a namaste, smile, and thank people when they offer you something.
What should I say when someone asks about my studies?
Answer simply and honestly, like, 'I'm in class ten and enjoying science.' Then ask them about something of theirs, and the conversation flows.
There's a colleague who is very quiet, and I'd like to include her more.
That's kind. Small steps work best. Ask for her opinion in meetings, or invite her to join for tea.
What if she says no?
Then be relaxed about it. Some people take time to warm up, and a friendly invitation now and then tells her the door is open.
I've started a small stall at the school fair with my friend, and we've no idea how to price our handmade bookmarks.
A simple way is to think about what the materials cost and what your classmates are likely to spend. Check with your teacher about any fair rules.
Should we sell them in sets?
A set of three, at a small saving over buying them one by one, can attract buyers. Display one set as a sample so people can see the colours.
I've just started learning to solve the cube puzzle and I'm stuck at the first layer.
The first layer is where most people struggle. Start with one colour, usually the one in the centre of a face, and build a cross.
I get the cross but the corners keep spoiling it.
Work on the corners one by one, placing each beside its matching edge pieces. A beginner's guide with pictures helps a lot, and you can find one in a library or online.
My back feels sore after carrying my school bag all week.
A heavy bag can make shoulders and back tired. Are both straps on your shoulders, and is the bag very full?
Only one strap, and it's quite heavy.
Wear both straps, keep the heaviest books close to your back, and take out whatever you don't need that day. If the soreness continues, tell a parent so a doctor can check.
I started a new book and the first chapter is already a little confusing.
First chapters often feel like walking into a room full of strangers. Do you know the setting or the characters yet?
Not really. There are lots of names.
A short list in the back of your notebook can help. Add each name and one detail. By the third chapter you will have your bearings.
Good idea. Should I reread the first chapter?
Only if you want to. Many readers push on, because later chapters explain what the opening left unclear.
Our teacher said we should keep a small notebook for new science words.
That's a good habit. Write the word, its meaning in your own words and a tiny sketch if it helps.
Should I add the spelling too?
Yes, write the spelling carefully and underline any tricky part. Seeing the shape of the word helps you recall it later.
I just wrote 'photosynthesis'. It looks so long.
It does look long, but you can split it into 'photo', 'synthe' and 'sis'. 'Photo' means light, and the whole word is about how plants make food using light.
Nice. How many words should I add per day?
Two or three is plenty. A few words you really remember are worth more than ten you forget by Friday.
I'll aim for three. Maybe I'll test myself on Sundays.
A Sunday quiz is a clever plan. Cover the meanings and see how many you can say aloud, then mark the ones to review.
I'm starting a new job next week where I'll have to use a phone to speak to customers. I'm shy on calls.
Many people feel that way at first, and it gets easier with practice. Do you know what you will be speaking about?
Mostly answering questions about orders.
Then prepare a short opening line, like, 'Good morning, this is Anita, how can I help?' Having that ready takes away the first-second jitters.
What if I don't know the answer?
Say, 'Let me check that for you,' and find out, or ask a colleague. Customers appreciate honesty more than a quick guess.
What if a customer is upset?
Stay calm, let the customer finish, and say you understand the problem. Then say what you can do. A steady, kind voice often calms the other person.
That helps. Do you have a tip for ending the call?
Summarise the next step in one sentence, thank them for calling and wish them a good day. A clear ending leaves a good impression.
We're going by train to visit relatives and my sister keeps asking me when we'll arrive.
Long journeys are tough on patient people too. What is the travel time?
About nine hours.
You could break it into parts, such as 'two stations, then lunch, then a nap, then the river bridge.' Having small milestones makes the time feel shorter.
She can't read the clock yet. Any way to show her?
Draw a line on paper with a few stops marked on it and let her put a sticker at each station you pass. She can see how far you have come.
Great idea. What can we do after lunch?
A card game, a short story from a book, or watching the view and counting something, like cows or bridges. A short nap might come naturally.
We've packed playing cards. Any simple game for a six-year-old?
Try 'Snap' or matching pairs. Both are easy to learn and quick to play. Let her win sometimes, so it stays fun.
My friends are coming over tomorrow and I want to serve something that's easy to make in bulk. We're eight people.
Pasta, a big pot of khichdi or pulao, or make-your-own wraps are all good for a group. Do any of them avoid certain foods?
One is vegetarian, the rest eat everything.
Then a vegetarian main dish suits everyone. A big pulao with raita works well. You can add a simple salad on the side.
I've never cooked that much rice.
Cook it in two batches if your pot is not big enough, and don't overfill the pot, so the rice has room to cook evenly. Keep it covered to stay warm.
Can I prepare things beforehand?
Yes. Chop vegetables, make the raita and wash the rice in the afternoon, then cook everything about an hour before the guests arrive.
I'll do that. Should I make dessert as well?
Something simple like fruit or ice cream from the shop is enough. You already have the main dish to focus on.
I think our pet turtle looks lonely in his tank.
It's kind of you to care. Turtles are often fine on their own, but different kinds have different needs. Do you know which kind he is?
I'm not sure, the shop didn't say.
Then a local vet who looks after small animals can tell you, and advise about his tank. A vet is the best person to ask, since each kind has special needs.
Meanwhile, can I do anything for him?
Make sure he has clean water, a place to climb out and rest, and a proper light and warm spot. Check your care sheet or ask the shop for those details.
He likes to stay under a rock. Is that bad?
Many turtles like a hiding place, so the rock is probably a good thing. If he stops eating or looks unwell, the vet is the person to call.
Okay. I'll ask the vet at the next visit. He's called Sheldon, by the way.
Sheldon is a great name for a turtle, calm and in no hurry. I hope the vet visit goes well.
My friend and I made a plan to play badminton at six tomorrow, but another friend asked me to the cinema at the same time.
That's a tricky spot. Which plan was made first?
Badminton, a few days ago.
Then I'd keep that one, since you gave your word. You can tell the other friend kindly that you're busy and suggest another day.
What if I really want to see the film?
You could ask your badminton friend honestly whether she'd move the game by an hour or two. If she says no, stay with the first plan.
She said she could play at five instead.
That solves it, then. You could play badminton at five and still make it to the cinema, if the timings allow. Check the film's start time first.
The show is at seven, so it works!
Both plans are on. Pack water for the game, and maybe a snack for the film.
My grandmother and I are planning to make a family recipe book. Where do we start?
What a wonderful project. A good first step is to list the dishes you want to include. Let her talk and you write.
She doesn't use measurements. She says 'a handful' and 'till it smells right'.
That's normal for family cooking. Cook the dish with her and note what you see. Use your own hand or a cup to measure a handful and write it down.
Should I add stories too?
Yes, a few lines about where the dish comes from, or who loved it, make the book more personal. Ask her about a special occasion for each dish.
We could add photos of the family eating it.
That would be lovely. Even old photographs, with a caption, would add a lot. Keep the originals safe and copy them if you can.
I'll start with her kheer. It's the best.
A great first page. Taste-test as you go, since the cook always deserves a helper.
I've been trying to improve my badminton smash but the shuttle goes straight into the net.
A smash that goes into the net usually means that you are hitting it too early or too flat. Try to meet the shuttle a bit higher and in front of you.
How do I know where to hit it?
Keep your eye on the shuttle and let it rise to its highest point before you swing. Reach up with your racket arm, and snap the wrist forward and down.
I still miss many.
Try this drill. Ask a friend to feed you high shuttles from the other side, and aim for the floor on the far side of the net. Count how many land and try to beat your score.
Should I do it every day?
Three or four times a week is enough. Rest days let your arm recover, which matters for your shoulder and wrist.
Thanks! I'll show my friend the drill.
Good plan. Take turns feeding each other, so you both practise, and keep it playful.
I've been feeling a bit left out lately because my friends talk about things I know nothing about.
That's a hard feeling, and many people go through it. What kind of things do they talk about?
Shows and games I've never watched or played.
Ask them about one of those things, since people enjoy explaining what they love. You may find that you like it, or at least you'll understand the jokes.
I'm scared I'll look dumb for asking.
Asking shows interest. You could say, 'I haven't seen it, what's it about?' It is a friendly question, not a silly one.
Okay. And if I don't like it?
That's fine. You don't have to like everything they do. You can still listen and share your own interests too.
I might invite them to my favourite board game.
Good idea. Sharing what you like makes it a two-way friendship, and it gives everyone something new to talk about.
We've got guests staying for a week and I need to give them my room. I'll sleep in the hall.
That's generous of you. It will feel odd for a few days, but it's temporary. What's the main thing worrying you?
I'll lose my privacy, and my things are in there.
Move your valuables and daily things to a drawer or a bag that you can keep with you. Leave the room tidy and clear a shelf for the guests.
The hall gets noisy in the morning.
A light sleep mask or earplugs can help, if your parents agree. You could also go to bed a little early and keep a quiet corner for studying elsewhere.
Where could I study?
Maybe at the dining table once breakfast is cleared, or at a neighbour's or a friend's place. Ask your parents which spot is quiet and suitable.
The dining table is fine in the afternoon.
Great, that gives you a workable plan. A week passes quickly, and you'll have your room back soon.
There's an anthill near our garden gate and I keep stepping near it. I don't want to hurt them.
Kind of you to think of them. Ants rebuild quickly, but it is nice to avoid stepping on the hill. Can you see where they walk?
They go in a line from the hill to a crack in the wall.
That's an ant trail. They follow a scent path left by earlier ants. If you step across it, they will find the line again after a short time.
Why do they walk in a line?
Each ant leaves a scent on the way, and the others follow it. That way, they can find food and go home without getting lost.
That is clever. What do they eat?
Many ants eat small crumbs, sweet things and tiny insects, depending on the kind. They carry food back to the hill to share.
I'll leave a tiny crumb a little away from the gate.
That will keep them away from your path, and it is fun to watch. Just a crumb, though, since a big pile can attract more insects.
I'm writing my first poem and I can't get it to rhyme.
Poems don't have to rhyme at all. Many fine poems don't. What is the poem about?
The rain on my window.
Then start by writing what you see and hear, in short lines. 'Drops tap on the glass' is already a line of poetry.
It sounds plain, though.
Plain can be powerful. To add colour, try comparing the rain to something, like a drum, or a tiny dancer. Use only one comparison, so it stays fresh.
I'll say the rain is a drummer. What comes after?
Tell us what the drummer plays, maybe a slow tune on the window and a quick one on the roof. Let your lines follow the feeling of the rain.
I like 'a drummer with no sticks'. It feels right.
It does, and it's your own idea, which is the best kind. Read the poem aloud and cut any word that doesn't help the picture.
My laptop keeps showing a message about low storage. I don't know what to delete.
Start with the things you know you don't need, such as duplicate downloads, old installers and big videos you've already watched or saved elsewhere.
How do I find the big ones?
Most computers can sort files by size, so check the biggest ones first. Look in the downloads and videos folders. Look but don't delete anything you don't recognise.
Some files have names I don't understand.
Leave those alone, or ask a grown-up or your school's computer teacher. System files can look strange but may be needed.
I found a lot of old movies I already watched.
Those are fine to remove if you won't watch them again. Empty the bin afterwards, because deleted files stay in it until you clear it.
Done, I got space back. Should I back up my photos?
Yes, copy them to an external drive or another safe place. It's a small effort that protects pictures you care about.
We have a long layover at an airport and I'm travelling with my little cousin.
A layover with a child can be fun with a plan. How long is it?
About four hours.
First, find your gate and note the time to be back. Then explore, look at the planes from the windows and find a spot with seats and a snack.
She gets worried about missing the flight.

Show her the departure board and your gate, so she can see where you need to be. Set an alarm for an hour before boarding, and let her hold the boarding passes if you trust her, so she feels responsible.
That's a good idea. What do we do for four hours?
Walk around the terminal, play a card game, draw or read. Take breaks for water and a snack, and let her rest if she is tired.
Can we get food at the airport?
Usually yes, but it can be pricey. Carrying fruit or a packed snack is cheaper and easier. Check the airline's rules about food first.
Our family is getting ready for Navratri, and I've been given the job of decorating the prayer corner.
Congratulations on the job. Do you know what your family usually puts there?
Flowers, lamps and a cloth, mostly.
Then you could keep that and add a fresh look with new flower garlands and a clean cloth. Ask elders if there are details they'd like to keep the same.
Where do I get flowers?
A local flower market or a vendor near a temple usually has them. Buy on the morning of the day, since fresh flowers last longer, and keep them cool until you use them.
What if I run out of time?
Keep it simple. A clean spot, a lamp and one garland can look just as beautiful as a big display. Ask a sibling or a cousin to help.
My cousin loves rangoli. She can do the floor.
Perfect, that completes the corner. Colours on the floor and flowers above will look wonderful together.
I've joined a small band at school. We're all beginners and we sound pretty bad.
Everybody starts there, and the joy of playing together is what counts. What do you play?
I play the drums. There's also a keyboard, a guitar and a singer.
Drums are the heartbeat of a band, so your steady beat helps everyone else. Practise keeping a slow, even rhythm first.
We keep speeding up during songs.
That is typical. Try playing along with a slow metronome or a recorded beat, and agree on one song to practise slowly.
How do we choose a song?
Pick something simple with a few chords and a clear beat. A song everybody knows will help you hear if you're off.
We'll try a simple one on Friday. Our band needs a name.
Names are fun to brainstorm. Let everyone write down three, and choose one you all like without long arguments.
My project partner wants to do everything his way and won't listen.
That's hard to deal with. Have you told him how you feel about it?
Not yet. I don't want a fight.
You don't need one. Try a calm line such as, 'I have a few ideas too. Can we try both and pick the best parts?' That keeps it fair.
What if he still says no?
Then you could ask your teacher for help in deciding together. Say it neutrally, like, 'We have different ideas and need advice.'
Alright. I'll start by sharing my ideas first.
Good start. Write them down so you can show them quickly, and be ready to like some of his ideas too.
My mother's birthday is on Sunday and I'd like to make her breakfast in bed.
A sweet gesture. What can you make comfortably?
Toast with jam and tea, maybe some cut fruit.
That will do nicely. Cut the fruit into small pieces, make the tea gently and put everything on a tray with a flower or a card.
Should I make it a surprise?
If she's a person who loves surprises, yes. You could ask your father or sibling to help you keep the secret, and wake her up with a gentle knock.
I'm afraid I'll spill the tea.
Fill the cup only two-thirds, walk slowly and set the tray down before you open the door. A saucer under the cup catches small spills.
I'll practise with water first. Thank you!
Excellent plan. A water rehearsal costs nothing and saves a lot of worry.
My dad signed me up for a swimming class and the water at the pool looks very deep.
Beginners often feel that. Classes start in the shallow end, and the instructor will be with you. Does the class have a trained instructor?
Yes, he's trained.
Good. Listen to his instructions and go at your own pace. It's fine to tell him you're nervous. He'll expect it.
What if I swallow water?
It happens to most beginners and it's usually just a cough and a laugh. Learning to blow bubbles out under water helps you control your breathing.
I'll practise blowing bubbles in the bathtub then.
That's a good warm-up. Try a gentle breath out through your mouth and nose, and go slowly.
I forgot to say thank you to my aunt for a gift and now it's been a week.
That happens, and a late thank-you is still very welcome. How did she send it?
She gave it to me at a family dinner.
Then a quick call or a short note will do nicely. You might say, 'I'm sorry I didn't say it earlier. Thank you for the lovely gift.'
Should I write or call?
Whichever feels more natural. A call is warm, and a written note can be kept. If you're shy, write something short and hand it to her.
I'll write a note and give it on Sunday.
That sounds lovely. Add a line about how you've been using the gift. She'll enjoy hearing it.
Our team meeting always runs very long, and nobody seems to get anything done.
Long meetings drain everyone. Is there an agenda?
No, we just start talking.
You could suggest a short list of topics before the meeting, and a time limit for each. A clear end time helps people stay focused.
I'm junior. Is it okay to suggest that?
You can phrase it as a question, like, 'Would a short agenda help us finish sooner?' That sounds helpful, not bossy.
I'll try it with my team lead first.
A sensible step. If she likes it, she can bring it up with the group, and you'll have helped without any awkwardness.
A lizard has been living behind the bathroom mirror and my sister is scared of it.
Small lizards are common in houses, and they usually eat insects. Does it come out much?
Only at night, near the light.
Then it's probably catching insects around the bulb. Most house lizards are harmless, and they leave on their own if you keep the bathroom dry and tidy.
My sister still won't go in.
You could keep the door open and the light on, and walk in first. Telling her what it eats can make it less scary, and your parents can help if it's a problem.
I'll tell her it's an insect catcher.
That's a friendly way to put it. She may even start to find it useful.
There's a big tree outside our school that loses all its leaves in winter. Is it dying?
Not necessarily. Many trees drop their leaves in the cold season and grow them again in spring. They do this to save energy and water.
But it looks so bare.
It does, but look closely at the branches. Small buds are often waiting to open when the weather warms.
Are there trees that stay green all year?
Yes, evergreen trees keep most of their leaves through the year. They shed old leaves a few at a time, so they never look fully bare.
Can we check the buds in winter?
Yes, look at the tips of the twigs, and compare them every few weeks. A small photo diary would show the tree waking up.
Two of my friends have stopped talking to each other and they both talk to me about the other.
That puts you in a hard spot. How do you feel about hearing both sides?
Uncomfortable. I don't want to take sides.
It's fair to tell them that. You could say, 'I care about you both, and I'd rather not talk about the other one. Maybe talk to each other?'
What if they get upset with me?
They may feel a little hurt at first, but most people respect a kind and honest boundary. Staying fair is a way to remain a good friend to both.
What if they ask me to deliver messages?
Politely decline, and suggest they speak for themselves. Messages passed on can get mixed up.
I'm learning to play the flute and my sound is more like a hiss.
Flutes are tricky at first. The sound depends on how the air is aimed at the edge of the hole. Are you holding the flute steady?
I think so.
Try tiny adjustments to the angle of your lips and breath. Make a small round opening and blow a thin, steady stream across the hole, not into it.
It still hisses.
Practise just the first note for a few minutes each day, and listen for when it rings. If you have a teacher, ask them to check your lip position.
I'll ask on Monday.
A good plan. A small correction from a teacher often fixes it in a minute.
My eyes get tired after a long time of reading in the evening.
Tired eyes after a long read are common. Is the light in your room bright enough?
It's a bit dim.
Brighter light behind or beside you can help, and so can short breaks. Look away at something far for a moment every half hour. If your eyes hurt a lot, tell your parents so an eye doctor can check.
Thanks. I'll move my lamp.
Go for it. Keep the lamp steady on your page, and your evening reading should feel easier.
I want to send my teacher a project file but it's too large for email.
Large files often don't fit as attachments. Does your school have a shared folder or class portal?
Yes, there's one.
Then upload it there, and send the teacher a short note that it's ready. Check the file opens properly before you tell her.
Good idea. I'll open it first and then upload.
That's the right order. Opening it first means your teacher will see a working file and you won't have to send it twice.
The bell rang before I finished my test paper, and I left two questions blank.
That's frustrating. Do you think you could have finished with a better plan?
I spent too long on one hard question.
Next time, try a first pass through the paper and answer the easy ones first. Mark the hard ones and return to them if you have time.
I'll try that. Should I tell the teacher what happened?
You can mention it kindly if you wish, but the main thing is to learn from it. A time check halfway through the test is a useful habit.
My dosa batter turned out too thick and it won't spread on the pan.
Thick batter is easy to fix. Stir in a little water, a spoonful at a time, until it flows like thin pancake batter.
Won't the dosa break then?
A thinner batter makes thin, crisp dosas, but a very runny one may tear. Aim for a smooth, pourable texture, and test with one dosa first.
The first one worked! It's a bit pale though.
Let the pan get a bit hotter before the next one, and wait until the edges lift. Golden colour comes from a hotter pan and a little patience.
I'd like to try skipping rope as a warm-up before cricket practice.
Good warm-up choice. It wakes up your legs and gets your heart going. Do you have a rope?
Yes, but I trip after ten jumps.
Keep your jumps small and stay on your toes. Turn the rope from your wrists, not your whole arms.
I'll try for a minute before practice tomorrow.
A minute is a good start. Build up slowly, and you'll soon be jumping past ten without thinking about it.
My friend gave me a handmade keychain, but it's not really my style.
That's a thoughtful gift, even if it isn't to your taste. You can still be grateful for the effort.
Should I tell her I don't like it?
No need. Thank her for making it, and appreciate the effort. You could clip it to the inside of your bag, where you can see it.
That works. She'll feel appreciated and I won't feel awkward.
Exactly. It's a small kindness that keeps the friendship warm and costs nothing.
Our school trip is to a fort, and I'm excited, but I don't know what to carry.
A fort trip means walking and climbing. A water bottle, a hat, comfortable shoes and a small snack are good basics.
What about a camera?
If your school allows it, a phone or a simple camera is fine. Keep it in a small bag and don't wander off to take photos alone. Stay with the group.
Right. And what if it rains?
Carry a light raincoat or a foldable poncho. Stone steps get slippery when wet, so wear shoes with a good grip.
I'd like to learn the drums but we have no space at home.
Drums are space-hungry, but you could start with a practice pad and sticks. They're small and quiet.
Can I really learn on a pad?
Yes. Rhythm, hand control and timing all develop on a pad. Many teachers start students that way. Ask a teacher to guide you with basic patterns.
I'll look for a teacher then. Thanks!
Good luck with the search. Meanwhile, tap simple beats on a cushion or a book with pencils, and your hands will start learning the patterns.
